text.p: Sunbeam Corp's huge $337 million write-off in the fourth quarter could be used to dress up the company's future results, but the accounting practices used could be described as "aggressive," Barron's reported.
By taking a charge in 1996, Sunbeam could cut provisions in 1997 and 1998 to reduce overall expenses, while reversing reserves could add profits, Barron's said.
No one at Sunbeam could be reached for comment on Sunday.

The boost to 1997's earnings from the charge could fade by 1998, which could lead to chairman Al Dunlap to make an acquisition to maintain the earnings growth or sell Sunbeam, said Barron's, a financial weekly.
Dunlap has said that he is willing to sell the company for the right price or he would make an acquisition.
Russell Kersh, executive vice president for finance and administration, denied that the company's motive behind the charge was to burnish operating results, Barron's said.
"Accounting regulations are strict on that score, and (Chairman Al Dunlap) has always been vehement about our doing things the right way," Kersh told the financial weekly.
The story also highlighted the challenges Dunlap faces at the small appliances maker and raised the issue of Sunbeam's restructuring to cut the company's payroll by half to 6,000 workers.
Of the $337 million write-off, $90 million was in inventory that could still have value, Barron's reported.

Sunbeam boosted a litigation charge by $17.7 million for a Superfund liability, increased doubtful accounts in 1996 to $23.4 million from $10.7 million in 1995, and took a $92 million charge on property, plant and equipment.
